title: From First Draft to Final Insight: A Multi-Agent Approach for Feedback Generation
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of generating large volumes of high-quality educational feedback using large language models (LLMs). The authors argue that while LLMs can automate feedback production, single-round feedback generation often suffers from problems such as hallucinations, verbosity, and weak alignment with pedagogical principles, especially learner-centered feedback. The study asks which prompt and framework combinations produce the best initial feedback, how accurately LLMs can evaluate generated feedback, and whether a multi-agent generation-evaluation-regeneration pipeline can improve feedback quality.

The intervention studied is a multi-agent LLM workflow called “G-E-RG” (generation, evaluation, and regeneration). In the first round, GPT-4o generated feedback using six combinations of prompt strategies and feedback frameworks: zero-shot versus RAG+Chain-of-Thought, crossed with no framework, a learner-centered framework, and a knowledge-transmission framework. A second GPT-4o agent automatically evaluated the generated feedback using a rubric covering reliability, learner-centered components, features, and simplicity. A third GPT-4o agent then regenerated feedback based on these evaluation results. Human research assistants also coded feedback quality and checked evaluation outputs.

The study was conducted in a graduate course, E-Learning Design Principles and Methods, at Carnegie Mellon University in Fall 2024. The dataset included 208 anonymous student responses drawn from 63 multiple-choice questions and one open-ended question. The educational context was course quiz feedback, with students as recipients of the generated feedback and instructors as the target users of the automation system. Because the data came from a single graduate course at one university, the context is specialized and narrow.

The main conclusion is that the multi-agent G-E-RG process substantially improved feedback quality across most measured dimensions regardless of the first-round generation method. Evaluation accuracy improved by roughly 3.36% to 12.98%, and regenerated feedback almost universally included the four desired learner-centered components. The RAG_CoT plus learner-centered framework produced the strongest first-round feedback, but the regeneration stage helped bring weaker methods up to a similarly strong level. However, the authors note remaining weaknesses in features such as positivity, usability, and relationship-building, and they emphasize that the pipeline is resource-intensive, depends on retrieval quality, and may still require human oversight for some evaluation dimensions.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: An OpenAI GPT-family large language model used here as the underlying engine for automated feedback generation, evaluation, and regeneration.
identified_tools.use_case: GPT-4o was used as three agents in a multi-agent 'G-E-RG' pipeline to generate first-round quiz feedback, automatically evaluate that feedback with a rubric, and regenerate improved second-round feedback for graduate course quiz responses.

findings.finding_summary: Across six prompt/framework methods, the multi-agent G-E-RG pipeline improved feedback evaluation accuracy from first- to second-round feedback by 3.36% to 12.98%. Improvements were statistically significant for all methods except RAG_CoT_knowledge, which showed a non-significant gain of 3.36% (p = 0.07); for example, RAG_CoT_learner reached 97.60% correct evaluation rate in round 2, a 6.73% improvement (p < 0.001).
findings.measure: Feedback evaluation accuracy against student responses
findings.effect_size: increase of 3.36% to 12.98% depending on method

findings.finding_summary: The proportion of feedback containing all four learner-centered components increased dramatically after regeneration, with second-round coverage ranging from 96.63% to 99.52% across methods. The paper also reports that coverage of individual components in second-round feedback reached 99.04% to 100%, with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests showing significant improvements for most component deficiencies (generally p < 0.001, with some p = 0.005 or p = 0.014).
findings.measure: Presence of learner-centered feedback components (critiques, strengths, actionable information, agency)
findings.effect_size: all-four-components rose from first-round average 27.72% to second-round average 98.49%

findings.finding_summary: Most learner-centered feature scores improved significantly after G-E-RG across methods (Wilcoxon p < 0.001 for most comparisons), though some dimensions remained suboptimal. The paper notes persistent room for improvement in F1-positive, F2-usable, and F3-relationship, with second-round feature means still only ranging from 2.39/3 to 2.63/3.
findings.measure: Learner-centered feedback features (positive affect, usability, relationship, dialogue, independence)

findings.finding_summary: LLM-based automatic evaluation using GPT-4o showed strong agreement with human coders on several rubric dimensions but weaker performance on others. Reported F1 scores were 0.93 for evaluation accuracy, 0.84 for retrieved slides accuracy, 0.97 for C2-strengths, 0.98 for C3-actionable, 0.99 for F4-dialogue, but only 0.75 for F2-usable and 0.73 for F5-independence.
findings.measure: Agreement between LLM-based and human feedback evaluation (accuracy/precision/recall/F1)
findings.effect_size: F1 scores 0.73 to 0.99 depending on sub-indicator

findings.finding_summary: The G-E-RG process changed feedback length, often condensing verbose outputs without losing core quality dimensions. Significant word-count reductions were observed for Baseline_learner (-25.77 words, p < 0.001), RAG_CoT_learner (-15.24, p < 0.001), and RAG_CoT_knowledge (-76.83, p < 0.001), while RAG_CoT_none increased by 20.34 words (p < 0.001) and Baseline_knowledge showed no significant change (p = 0.439).
findings.measure: Feedback simplicity measured by word count
findings.effect_size: mean change ranged from -76.83 to +20.34 words depending on method

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical evaluation of a multi-agent LLM feedback pipeline, but it is not an RCT or QED on student learning outcomes. The study mainly assesses generated feedback quality and rubric agreement within one course dataset.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports clear positive improvements in feedback quality metrics, but effects are on proxy outcomes rather than direct student learning, and standardized effect sizes are not reported. Impact appears promising but remains unclear in magnitude for educational outcomes.
